topic.title: Define a concurrency model (aka memory model) for Python
topic.text:
Over the years there have been attempts to define a memory model, notably PEP 583 and many questions both on the bug tracker and here about expected semantics and atomicity of operations, e.g. What is Thread Safety as applied to Python? and What is the Long-Term Vision for a Parallel Python Programming Model?

Despite that, there is AFAICT, nothing in the docs.

We have an object model but there is no mention of concurrent access.

We should write down concurrency models for both with-GIL and free-threading Python.

It doesn’t need to be super precise and ultra rigorous, just reasonably complete and unambiguous.

To start with it doesn’t even need to be that. Once we have a core, details can be filled out:

Sticking with the with GIL build, the basic threading model should cover:

What is the GIL.

Properties of the GIL

The state of threads when releasing or acquiring the GIL

Which of the most common operations are atomic

How to describe the behavior of non-atomic operations

Comparison to archetypal memory models, like Sequential Consistency.

How much leeway other implementations, like MIcroPython and GraalPython have

and other things as necessary.

reason: PEP 583 (A Concurrency Memory Model for Python, 2008) covered the same idea; it was withdrawn by its authors. The graph records no ruling for PEP 583, only its status (Withdrawn); the reply says so and where the discussion stopped. Nobody active found; a moderator should pick reviewers.

evidence.title: A Concurrency Memory Model for Python

draft:
This has come up before.

- PEP 583 ("A Concurrency Memory Model for Python", 2008) proposed it (This PEP describes how Python programs may behave in the presence of concurrent reads and writes to shared variables from multiple threads.) https://peps.python.org/pep-0583/
  No ruling is recorded for it: it was withdrawn by its authors. The discussion stopped there.

No ruling was recorded, so a new proposal would start from where that discussion stopped. People who know this history: Jeffrey Yasskin.

(Drafted by Lineage from the PEP graph. Check the links before posting.)
